title: Dependency Injection Framework
seoTitle: Design an IoC / Dependency Injection Framework
description: Design an inversion-of-control container — registering bindings, resolving dependency graphs, lifetimes and scopes, cycle detection, and fast resolution.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is a Dependency Injection Framework?
blocks.text: A dependency injection (DI) container builds objects for you. Instead of classes creating their own dependencies, they declare what they need, and the container constructs and wires them — think Spring, Guice, or .NET's built-in container.

items: Developers should be able to register bindings: an interface → an implementation (or a factory, or an instance).
The container should resolve an object by constructing it and all its dependencies recursively.
Bindings should support lifetimes: transient (new each time), singleton (one per container), and scoped (one per request/scope).
The container should report clear errors for missing bindings and circular dependencies.

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this framework?

items: Resolution must be fast — it may run on every request in a web server.
Thread-safe: concurrent resolution must never create two singletons.
Fail fast: configuration errors should surface at startup, not in production traffic.
Small, predictable API that's easy to test with.
**Binding**: service key (type/token) → provider (class, factory, or instance) + lifetime.
**Container**: holds bindings and singleton instances; builds objects.
**Scope**: a child container holding scoped instances (e.g. per HTTP request).
**Resolution plan**: a precompiled recipe for constructing a type.

blocks.text: `bind()` records a Binding in a map keyed by the service token. Dependencies of each implementation are discovered from constructor metadata (type annotations / decorators, or an explicit `inject` list), so the container knows what each class needs.
`resolve(T)` looks up T's binding, resolves each constructor dependency first (depth-first), then constructs T. The result is a directed acyclic graph of objects.

items: **Transient**: construct a new instance every time.
**Singleton**: construct once, cache in the root container, reuse forever.
**Scoped**: construct once per scope (stored in the scope's cache), disposed when the scope ends.

blocks.text: A scope delegates singleton lookups to its root, so singletons are shared while scoped instances stay per-request.
Missing bindings throw with the full resolution path ("UserService → UserRepo → DbPool: no binding for Config"). Cycles are detected by tracking the stack of types currently being resolved.
1) How do we detect configuration errors early?

approach.text: Only fail when a request happens to need a broken binding.

challenges.text: Errors appear in production, possibly hours after deploy.

blocks.title: Validate the whole graph at startup

approach.text: `validate()` walks every registered binding's dependency graph without constructing objects, checking that every dependency has a binding, detecting cycles (DFS with a "visiting" set), and flagging **captive dependencies** — a singleton depending on a scoped service, which would leak one request's object into all requests.

challenges.text: Factories are opaque; require them to declare their dependencies so they can be validated too.

blocks.text: 2) How do we make resolution fast?

approach.text: Inspect constructor metadata each time an object is built.

challenges.text: Reflection is slow when repeated on hot paths.

approach.text: On first use (or at validation), compile each binding into a **resolution plan** — effectively a generated factory function that calls dependency factories directly. Cache plans by type; subsequent resolves are just function calls and cache lookups.

challenges.text: Plans must be invalidated if bindings change, which is why bindings are frozen after startup.

blocks.text: 3) How do we keep singletons thread-safe?

Use double-checked locking (or a per-binding lazy initializer) so only one thread constructs a singleton and others wait for it. Avoid holding a global lock during construction — a singleton's constructor might resolve other singletons, and a global lock would deadlock or serialise everything.

quiz.question: What is a captive dependency?
options: A longer-lived service (singleton) holding a shorter-lived one (scoped)
quiz.explanation: The scoped object would leak across requests.

quiz.question: How are circular dependencies detected?
options: Tracking types currently being resolved and erroring if one repeats
quiz.explanation: A type appearing twice on the resolution stack means a cycle.

quiz.question: Why validate the container at startup?
options: So configuration errors fail the deploy instead of production requests

quiz.question: What makes repeated resolution fast?
quiz.explanation: Plans turn resolution into direct function calls.
